fields.resolution_rationale:
The baptism year of Sarah Hollins reads 1746 in the original Bolton-le-Moors parish register (a_001) and 1747 in a printed transcript of the same register (a_002). This one-year discrepancy must be explained before a date can be recorded.

The original entry (a_001) was made by the parish curate at or shortly after the baptism — the strongest possible informant for a contemporaneous church event. The transcript (a_002) was produced by a later transcriber working from the same register page; it is secondary information, not a new witness. Every other detail — 14 February, Bolton-le-Moors, father William Hollins — is identical in both sources.

This is not a genuine informant disagreement. England operated under an Old Style civil year beginning 25 March until the Calendar (New Style) Act took effect in September 1752. Dates between 1 January and 24 March were assigned the lower year number in registers of that era. The mandatory convert_calendar check (osNsYear, jurisdiction: England) applied to 14 February 1746 returns 14 February 1747 New Style — exactly what a_002 records. The two dates name the same calendar day. The original register (a_001) is preferred as the authoritative primary-information source; the curate wrote 1746 because Old Style convention required it, and that entry is correct within the regime in force at the time. The New Style equivalent — the year to record in a modern family history — is 1747, and the date may be expressed as 14 February 1746/7 to preserve transparency about the original.

The transcript's 1747 is not an error. Parish register transcription societies — including the Lancashire Parish Register Society — routinely advanced the year by one for pre-1752 January–March dates when publishing printed transcripts, bringing them into alignment with the modern civil year so readers unfamiliar with Old Style reckoning would not be misled. The transcriber was faithfully reporting the same event as the curate; the difference is purely notational, arising from the well-documented calendar-convention change of 1752.

However, a one-year age difference falls squarely within normal census recording variation and carries no diagnostic weight. Using the Thomas Flynn relationship to confirm the identity is circular reasoning — it assumes the very thing being questioned. No record outside the 1850 census independently names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father, and no record has been found placing our subject in either household at a later date.

fields.weighing_analysis:
Two Patrick Flynns appear in 1850 Schuylkill County: household 84 (Thomas Flynn's household, Patrick age 5, born ~1845) and household 197 (Patrick age 6, born ~1844). Co-enumeration confirms they were distinct individuals, but does not by itself identify which became our subject.

The 1860 census (a_009, a_010) provides the decisive bridging evidence: Patrick Flynn, age ~15, continues to live in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. An age of 15 in 1860 implies birth ~1845, matching household 84's Patrick (born ~1845) and not household 197's Patrick (born ~1844, who would have been ~16 in 1860). The age trajectory across a decade positively distinguishes the Thomas Flynn household child from the other same-named contemporary.

The 1908 death certificate (a_013) names Thomas Flynn directly as father of the deceased Patrick Flynn, who died in Schuylkill County — completing the chain. Birth year ~1845 is stable across all three records. The United States Naming Customs wiki page confirms no patronymic system applies; surname evidence carries standard weight only.

Because the 1850 census does not record family relationships, the child's tie to Thomas Flynn in that record is inferred from household position and shared surname alone — which raised a genuine question about whether this is the Patrick Flynn who died in 1908.

On one side, a_001 places Patrick Flynn as a child in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household (age 5, born ~1845) in Schuylkill County. On the other, the 1908 death certificate (src_004, a_013) reports Thomas Flynn as the deceased's father — information supplied by James Brown (son-in-law), who received it indirectly. In between, the 1860 census (a_009, a_010) records Patrick Flynn, age ~15, still in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household.

The 1860 census is the decisive bridging record. An age of 15 in 1860 implies birth ~1845, which matches household 84's Patrick exactly and excludes household 197's Patrick (born ~1844, who would have been ~16). This positive age-and-location continuity within Thomas Flynn's household distinguishes our subject from the co-enumerated same-name contemporary and provides direct placement — not an argument from the alternative's absence.

With three independent records in the same county, a stable birth year, a coherent age trajectory, and a death certificate directly naming Thomas Flynn as father, the evidence preponderates that a_001 records our research subject. The conflict existed because a second Patrick Flynn of similar age appeared in the same county at the same date; the 1860 bridging record, combined with the age differential (household 84: born ~1845 vs. household 197: born ~1844), resolves the ambiguity positively in favor of the Thomas Flynn household child.
